explainers.title: Why do district maps change?
text: The Constitution divides the 435 House seats among the states by population, counted every ten years by the census. When a state's share of the nation's population grows or shrinks, it can gain or lose seats, and it must redraw its districts to match.

Even when a state keeps the same number of seats, people move. Since the Supreme Court's 1964 decision in Wesberry v. Sanders, each state's districts must have nearly equal populations, so states with more than one seat redraw after every census.

Maps also change when a court finds a map unlawful, for example because it breaks the Voting Rights Act or a state constitution, and orders a new one. And some states have redrawn in the middle of a decade, without a new census.
Who draws the lines depends on the state: usually the legislature, but in some states an independent or bipartisan commission, and sometimes a court when the others cannot agree.

explainers.title: What is gerrymandering?
text: Gerrymandering means drawing district lines to give one group an advantage over another, such as one party, or to weaken the voting strength of a racial or ethnic group.

Two common techniques are "packing", putting as many of one group's voters as possible into a few districts, and "cracking", spreading them thinly across many districts so they are outnumbered in each.
The word dates from 1812, when Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry signed a state senate map with a district that a newspaper cartoon compared to a salamander.

The Supreme Court has held that drawing districts mainly by race without a strong justification is unconstitutional (Shaw v. Reno, 1993), and that federal courts cannot decide claims of partisan gerrymandering (Rucho v. Common Cause, 2019). State courts and state constitutions can still limit partisan maps.

explainers.title: What is the shape score?
text: The map shows a Polsby-Popper compactness score for each district: 4π × area ÷ perimeter², from 0 to 1. A circle scores 1; long, thin or winding shapes score lower.

The score measures shape only. A low score can come from coastlines, rivers, county lines or keeping communities together, not just from gerrymandering, so it is not proof of anyone's intent. "Notably irregular" marks the least compact districts of each era by this measure.

milestones.title: The Constitution sets up apportionment
milestones.text: Article I says House seats are divided among the states by population, counted in a census every ten years, with at least one seat per state.

milestones.title: First apportionment
milestones.text: After a veto by President Washington of an earlier bill, Congress passed the first apportionment act, dividing 105 seats among the states using the 1790 census.

milestones.title: Apportionment Act of 1842
milestones.text: Congress required states with more than one seat to elect members from single-member districts made of contiguous territory, ending statewide general tickets in law. Four states still elected their members statewide in 1842 and 1843, and the House seated them.

milestones.title: The House reaches 435 seats
milestones.text: The apportionment after the 1910 census set the House at 433 seats plus one each for Arizona and New Mexico on admission, 435 in all. The act required districts to be compact, contiguous and equal in population.

milestones.title: No reapportionment after the 1920 census
milestones.text: Congress did not pass an apportionment law after the 1920 census, so seats stayed as set after 1910 for the rest of the decade.

milestones.title: Permanent Apportionment Act
milestones.text: Congress fixed the House at 435 seats and made reapportionment automatic after each census. The act had no rules on drawing districts, which let states elect members at-large again.

milestones.title: Wood v. Broom
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that the earlier federal requirements for compact, contiguous, equal districts had lapsed with the 1929 act.

milestones.title: Method of equal proportions
milestones.text: Congress adopted the method of equal proportions, the formula still used to divide seats among the states.

milestones.title: Colegrove v. Green
milestones.text: The Supreme Court upheld the dismissal of a challenge to Illinois's unequal congressional districts; a plurality called districting a political question.

milestones.title: Baker v. Carr
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that federal courts can hear claims that unequally populated districts violate the Equal Protection Clause.

milestones.title: Wesberry v. Sanders
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that congressional districts within a state must have populations as nearly equal as practicable ("one person, one vote").

milestones.title: Reynolds v. Sims
milestones.text: The Supreme Court applied the equal-population rule to both houses of state legislatures.

milestones.title: Voting Rights Act
milestones.text: Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, which bars voting practices, including district maps, that discriminate on the basis of race. Some states also had to get federal approval before changing maps.

milestones.title: Single-member districts required
milestones.text: A federal law required every state with more than one seat to use single-member districts, ending general-ticket and at-large elections for those states, with short-term exceptions for Hawaii and New Mexico.

milestones.title: Kirkpatrick v. Preisler
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that there is no fixed population difference between congressional districts that is automatically acceptable.

milestones.title: Voting Rights Act amended
milestones.text: Congress amended Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act so that a map can be unlawful if it has a discriminatory result, even without proof of discriminatory intent.

milestones.title: Karcher v. Daggett
milestones.text: The Supreme Court struck down a New Jersey map whose population differences were under 1%, because the state did not justify them.

milestones.title: Thornburg v. Gingles
milestones.text: The Supreme Court set the test for when a map illegally dilutes minority votes under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act.

milestones.title: Shaw v. Reno
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that voters can challenge a district drawn so irregularly that it can be explained only by race.

milestones.title: Miller v. Johnson
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that a district is subject to strict review when race was the predominant factor in drawing it.

milestones.title: Vieth v. Jubelirer
milestones.text: The Supreme Court rejected a partisan gerrymandering claim against Pennsylvania's map; a plurality found no workable standard to judge such claims.

milestones.title: LULAC v. Perry
milestones.text: The Supreme Court upheld most of Texas's 2003 mid-decade map, holding that a state may redraw between censuses, but found one district violated the Voting Rights Act.

milestones.title: Shelby County v. Holder
milestones.text: The Supreme Court struck down the formula that decided which places needed federal approval before changing voting rules, including maps.

milestones.title: Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that voters may give congressional map drawing to an independent commission.

milestones.title: Cooper v. Harris
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that two North Carolina districts were racial gerrymanders.

milestones.title: Rucho v. Common Cause
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions that federal courts cannot decide.

milestones.title: Allen v. Milligan
milestones.text: The Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Alabama's map likely violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and reaffirmed the Gingles test.

milestones.title: Moore v. Harper
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that state courts may review congressional maps under their state constitutions.

milestones.title: Alexander v. South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP
milestones.text: The Supreme Court reversed a ruling that a South Carolina district was a racial gerrymander, holding that challengers had not shown race rather than politics drove its lines.

milestones.title: A wave of mid-decade redistricting
milestones.text: Starting in 2025, several states redrew their congressional maps without a new census, including Texas, California, Missouri, North Carolina and Ohio (whose constitution required a new map), followed in 2026 by Florida, Tennessee and Louisiana. A court replaced Utah's map, Alabama returned to its 2023 map, voters rejected Missouri's new map, and other redraws failed.

milestones.title: Louisiana v. Callais
milestones.text: The Supreme Court held that the Voting Rights Act did not require Louisiana to draw a second majority-Black district, and that the district it drew was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.

milestones.title: The 2026 election
milestones.text: Members of the 120th Congress were elected on November 3, 2026, still under the 2020 census apportionment: each state kept the same number of seats as in 2022 and 2024, 435 in all. Nine states used a different congressional map than in 2024: Alabama, California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah.
